title: Does Birth Order Shape Personality?
text:
Few beliefs about family are as popular as the idea that birth order shapes who we become: firstborns are responsible and bossy, middle children are diplomats, the youngest are charming rebels. Researchers had argued about it for a century, but many earlier studies compared people from different families or relied on siblings rating each other.

In 2015, Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff and Stefan Schmukle at the University of Leipzig analyzed data from more than 20,000 people in three large national surveys from Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States. They looked at standard personality traits such as extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness. Crucially, they compared not only people from different families but also brothers and sisters within the same family.

The result was clear. Birth order had no meaningful effect on extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness or conscientiousness. The only consistent effect was on intellect: firstborns scored very slightly higher on intelligence tests and rated themselves slightly higher on intellect, a difference of about one or two IQ points between neighboring siblings, too small to notice in any individual family.

Around the same time, another large study by Damian and Roberts reached similar conclusions.
lesson: Do not let birth order write your children's script. Siblings differ, but not in the way family folklore says, so look at each child as they are.
people: Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff, Stefan Schmukle
source: Rohrer, J. M., Egloff, B., and Schmukle, S. C. (2015). Examining the effects of birth order on personality. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(46), 14224-14229.
